title: The Restarting API
brief: Checkout requests began failing after a routine deployment. The pod starts, exits, and restarts continuously.

commands.kubectl get pods:
NAME                         READY   STATUS             RESTARTS
checkout-api-7d8f6c9-x2k4p  0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   8
commands.kubectl describe pod:
State: Waiting — CrashLoopBackOff
Last State: Terminated — Error (exit code 1)
Environment from: checkout-secrets (Secret)
Warning Failed: secret checkout-secrets not found
commands.kubectl logs: Error: required environment variable DATABASE_URL is not set
commands.kubectl logs --previous: FATAL startup validation failed: DATABASE_URL missing

hints: Start with pod status, then inspect events.
The application expects configuration from a Kubernetes Secret.
Compare the referenced Secret name with the Secrets that exist.
diagnosis: The Deployment references a missing checkout-secrets Secret, so DATABASE_URL is absent and the container exits.
remediation: Create the correctly named Secret or update secretRef, then restart and verify the rollout.
case_study: A Helm values rename changed the generated Secret name without updating the Deployment. Admission-time policy checking for missing references would have prevented the outage.

title: Healthy Pods, Dead Service
brief: Pods are healthy, but requests to the catalog Service time out from every namespace.
symptoms: All catalog pods are Running and Ready
curl to the Service times out
objectives: Explain why traffic has no backend

commands.kubectl get pods:
NAME                       READY   STATUS
catalog-6cbfd8f9b7-p9x2m    1/1     Running
catalog-6cbfd8f9b7-r5t8n    1/1     Running
commands.kubectl get svc:
NAME      TYPE       CLUSTER-IP    PORT(S)
catalog   ClusterIP  10.43.22.18   80/TCP

hints: A Service routes only to selected Ready pods.
Check whether the Service has endpoints.
Compare pod labels to the Service selector character-for-character.
diagnosis: The Service selects app=catalog while pods are labeled app=catalog-api, leaving the Service with no endpoints.
remediation: Change the Service selector to app=catalog-api and confirm endpoints populate before testing traffic.
case_study: A team standardized application labels but deployed the Service from an older manifest. Pods looked healthy, delaying diagnosis until endpoints were checked.

title: Image That Never Arrives
brief: A new worker release never starts after the pipeline reports a successful deployment.
objectives: Choose a safe rollback or repair

commands.kubectl describe pod:
Failed to pull image registry.local/worker:build-418
manifest unknown
Back-off pulling image

hints: Pod events usually explain image pull failures.
Differentiate authentication failure from a missing manifest.
Check whether the referenced tag exists.
diagnosis: The Deployment references worker:build-418, but that image manifest was never published to the registry.
remediation: Publish the immutable build-418 image or roll back to revision 12/build-417, then verify rollout status.
case_study: The deployment job ran even though the image publishing job was skipped. A pipeline dependency and registry existence gate would prevent this.

title: Alive but Never Ready
brief: The reports application runs, yet Kubernetes refuses to send it traffic after a framework upgrade.
objectives: Correct the probe without hiding failures

commands.kubectl describe pod:
Readiness probe failed: HTTP probe returned statuscode: 404
Path: /health
Port: 8080
commands.kubectl logs:
Server listening on :8080
Health endpoint mounted at /healthz

hints: Running and Ready are different conditions.
Compare the configured probe path with the path logged by the app.
diagnosis: The readiness probe requests /health, but the upgraded application exposes /healthz, causing 404 responses and no Ready endpoints.
remediation: Update readinessProbe.httpGet.path to /healthz, deploy, and confirm Ready endpoints before removing the old replica.
case_study: A framework upgrade renamed the default health route. Testing the deployment manifest against the built image would have caught the mismatch.

title: Unschedulable Memory Giant
brief: An analytics pod has remained Pending since its resource limits were tuned.
symptoms: Pod stays Pending with no node assignment

commands.kubectl describe pod:
Requests: memory 16Gi, cpu 2
Warning FailedScheduling: 0/2 nodes are available: 2 Insufficient memory
commands.kubectl get nodes:
NAME       STATUS   ROLES
control    Ready    control-plane
worker-1   Ready    <none>

hints: Pending pods often require scheduler-event inspection.
Resource requests, not limits, govern initial placement.
The pod requests more memory than any node can offer.
diagnosis: The analytics pod requests 16Gi of memory, exceeding the allocatable memory of every node, so the scheduler cannot place it.
remediation: Set a measured request the workload can use safely or add an appropriately sized node; then monitor actual usage and OOM events.
case_study: A developer copied production resource values into a small staging cluster. Environment-specific sizing and policy bounds were missing.

title: Ingress to Nowhere
brief: Internal Service access works, but the public hostname returns the ingress controller's default 404 page.
objectives: Separate DNS, routing, and backend failures

commands.kubectl get ingress:
NAME      CLASS     HOSTS
frontend  traefik   shop.internal.local
commands.curl:
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Request host: shop.richmack.local

hints: A controller 404 often means no routing rule matched.
The backend works from inside the cluster.
Compare the request Host header with spec.rules.host.
diagnosis: The request uses shop.richmack.local while the Ingress only matches shop.internal.local, so Traefik selects no route and returns its default 404.
remediation: Change the Ingress host or DNS/client URL to one canonical hostname, apply it, and test with the correct Host header.
case_study: Infrastructure and application teams used different environment domain conventions. A shared hostname value and post-deploy smoke test would catch the drift.
